text:
Adobe has completed its acquisition of Topaz Labs, the company behind the popular AI upscaling, sharpening and noise reduction tools used by many photographers and video editors. The deal was first announced in June and closed on 23 September.

The key news for existing Topaz users is that Topaz Labs will continue as a standalone brand, with its apps and models remaining available as separate products. That should reassure the many photographers who use Topaz software alongside Lightroom, Capture One or other editors, and who were vocal on the Topaz community forums about not wanting to be pushed into a Creative Cloud subscription.

What changes

Adobe says Topaz’s image and video enhancement models will be integrated into Adobe Firefly and Photoshop, with upscaling and image enhancement the first areas to benefit. It also plans to bring the technology into more Creative Cloud workflows over time, citing video upscaling, archival restoration and low-light enhancement.

Topaz’s Neurostream technology, which allows AI models to run either on-device or in the cloud, is also part of the deal. Topaz won an Emmy Award for video technology in 2025, and Adobe highlights its role in helping studios and broadcasters restore and remaster legacy footage for modern high-resolution platforms.

Topaz Labs CEO Eric Yang is joining Adobe’s Digital Video and Audio team.

“The best creative tools remove technical barriers so creators can focus on what matters most: telling stories that connect with audiences,” said Deepa Subramaniam of Adobe.

Our take

Adobe hasn’t said anything about pricing or licensing changes for current Topaz customers, and that’s the detail most photographers will be watching. Topaz moved to a subscription model of its own before the deal, so the question now is whether the standalone apps continue to be developed at the same pace once the best models also sit inside Photoshop. For now, it’s business as usual for Topaz users, and Photoshop users look set to get noticeably better upscaling.

Adobe and Topaz Labs deal key points

Acquisition announced June 2026, completed 23 September 2026

Topaz Labs remains a standalone brand; apps and models still sold separately

Topaz models to be integrated into Adobe Firefly and Photoshop

Future plans include video upscaling, archival restoration and low-light enhancement in Creative Cloud

Topaz CEO Eric Yang joins Adobe’s Digital Video and Audio team

However, the company is looking to replicate Office 365’s success by positioning Copilot as an AI productivity tool for its core enterprise user base. “Just as Office defined work for the PC era, the new Copilot is built to define it for the AI era,” Jared Spataro, chief marketing officer of AI at work at Microsoft, was quoted as saying by The Verge.

The new Home and Code tabs in Copilot will be rolled out in the coming weeks to those who are part of Microsoft’s Frontier programme for early access AI features. Autopilot will be rolled out in private preview later this month, while the Code tab will also be in preview for Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers later this year.

In terms of pricing, the Cowork, Code, and Autopilot parts of this new Copilot app will have usage-based billing. Users who have purchased a regular Copilot license will have access to Copilot in Chat, and in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams.

New Copilot features

The Home tab in the redesigned Copilot app will offer features previously available in Copilot Chat and Cowork. Under this section, Microsoft is also planning to launch a new ‘Today’ feature that will serve as a personalised dashboard for important emails, meeting requests, Teams threads, and more.

The super app’s Code tool will let users generate an app, tracker, dashboard, etc, and share the results with colleagues as cloud-hosted internal apps. The AI coding tool is powered by the same models underpinning GitHub Copilot and will run in a sandboxed environment as a security precaution.

Previously referred to as Scout, which was only available as a desktop app, the rebranded AI assistant has been reworked to function as a ‘digital teammate’ that can keep running even when users are asleep.

“Autopilot lives in your tenant with its own identity, memory, computer, and workspace, and it’s built on Microsoft IQ so it understands how your organization actually works. Under the hood, Autopilot appears to be built on top of several AI models with an auto model picker designed to route each task to a specific model.

text:
Eli Lilly has broken ground on a $6.5bn pharmaceutical manufacturing facility in Houston, Texas, as part of the company’s drive to expand domestic production of medicines and active pharmaceutical ingredients (API).

The Houston site is one of 10 US manufacturing facilities Lilly has announced since 2020 and will be the company’s fifth US location dedicated to API production. It will manufacture Foundayo (orforglipron), Lilly’s first synthetic oral GLP-1 medicine, alongside other small-molecule medicines and advanced therapeutics. The investment forms part of Lilly’s broader $50bn programme to expand US manufacturing capacity, aimed at meeting growing domestic demand while increasing the company’s ability to export medicines manufactured in the US.

“We are thrilled to break ground on our latest ‘medicines made in America’ site in the great state of Texas,” said David A. Ricks, Lilly chair and CEO.

“This $6.5bn investment will help change the game for tens of millions of people suffering from overweight, obesity and its consequences like diabetes. We will make and ship Lilly’s latest products from Texas to people here at home and around the world.”

Scaling next-generation medicines

Foundayo is a GLP-1 receptor agonist approved in the US for weight management in adults with obesity, or those who are overweight with a weight-related condition. Unlike peptide-based GLP-1 medicines, Foundayo is a small molecule, which Lilly says can be manufactured using more established technologies and is therefore more readily scalable. The drug is currently under regulatory review in more than 40 countries, with Lilly targeting a global rollout in 2027. The company is also investigating the medicine for applications including type 2 diabetes and obstructive sleep apnea.

The Houston facility will also produce advanced therapeutics including oligonucleotides, a class of medicines designed to act at the genetic level by switching off the production of specific proteins. Lilly said the facility will incorporate machine learning, artificial intelligence, digitally integrated systems and advanced data analytics to support manufacturing operations and improve right-first-time execution. Digital automation will be integrated throughout the site to streamline production and support the consistent supply of medicines meeting safety and quality requirements.

Building Houston’s manufacturing workforce

The project is expected to create more than 600 high-wage permanent jobs spanning engineering, science, operations and laboratory roles, while approximately 4,000 construction jobs will be created as the facility is built and brought online.

Lilly is also investing in developing the local workforce. The company is providing $12.5m to support a partnership with San Jacinto College, creating training pathways into advanced chemical synthesis manufacturing for people without prior industry experience. The programme will help train technicians, operators, maintenance professionals and other manufacturing workers, while Lilly specialists will contribute to curriculum development and instructor preparation.

A further $2.5m charitable donation to the San Jacinto College Foundation will support scholarships for eligible students.

“When you invest in a place like Houston, you invest in its people first,” said Edgardo Hernandez, executive vice president and president of Lilly Manufacturing Operations.

“This facility will run on the talent of this community, powered by our relationship with San Jacinto College.”

Lilly’s wider US manufacturing expansion includes facilities for API production in Richmond, Virginia; Huntsville, Alabama; Houston; and two locations in Lebanon, Indiana. The company is also developing facilities for injectable medicines and devices in North Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, alongside a genetic medicines facility in Lebanon, Indiana.

The Houston project adds further capacity to Lilly’s US manufacturing footprint as the pharmaceutical sector invests in domestic production of increasingly complex medicines.

text:
On September 25, Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) announced a comprehensive overhaul of its Copilot ecosystem, introducing a central workspace structure consisting of Home, Code, and Autopilot. Home unifies conversation and productivity tools by natively integrating Word, Excel, and PowerPoint into the Copilot interface. Code allows non-technical employees to build custom applications and automations using natural language powered by GitHub Copilot technology.

Meanwhile, Autopilot establishes persistent, proactive AI agents capable of carrying out continuous background workflows independently. To help enterprise IT leaders manage consumption, Microsoft simultaneously introduced FinOps for AI spend management controls.

You Might Also Want To Read: Azure's Inflection Point: Can Microsoft (MSFT) Balance AI Growth With Capex Risk?

Ken Wolter / Shutterstock.com

The Bull Case: Monetization, Platform Lock-In, and Cloud Integration

From a bullish perspective, expanding Copilot into no-code app building and persistent autonomous agents significantly strengthens Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)'s enterprise moat. Integrating GitHub Copilot's underlying technology directly into daily workplace tools extends solution-building capabilities to all knowledge workers, unlocking new seat licensing and usage-based monetization potential across its commercial client base.

Furthermore, these agentic and coding capabilities directly reinforce Microsoft's core growth drivers: Azure and Microsoft Cloud. Persistent agents running complex workflows require substantial compute, which translates into recurring Azure infrastructure usage. By embedding continuous agentic workflows and full Office integration deeper into enterprise operations, Microsoft enhances customer retention, boosts cross-selling opportunities across Microsoft 365 and Dynamics, and protects its high-margin software ecosystem through deep balance sheet liquidity and cloud dominance.

The Bear Case: Capital Intensity, Margin Compression, and Segment Drag

Conversely, bears view the rollout of continuous, persistent AI agents like Autopilot as a double-edged sword. Running autonomous agents that operate perpetually in the background—even when users are offline—demands an exceptionally heavy AI capital expenditure load. Microsoft's AI infrastructure spend is already accelerating faster than near-term free cash flow, raising concerns about capital efficiency and return on invested capital timelines.

Additionally, servicing complex code generation and persistent compute carries higher usage-related COGS and bandwidth requirements than traditional SaaS licensing. This cost structure risks exacerbating AI-driven gross margin compression across the Cloud division. If adoption relies heavily on usage-based credits, corporate IT departments using the newly introduced FinOps tools might restrict consumption to cap costs. Combined with ongoing softness in Windows OEM hardware demand and Xbox gaming hardware pressure, margin drag from heavy AI inference could dilute broader profitability.

text:
Microsoft and chip company Qualcomm launched the "Copilot+" PC branding in 2024 for so-called "AI" PCs. They even had a "Copilot" button that you could press to bring up the "AI". Though it at least indicated decent hardware, it was a hamfisted grasp at a vague buzzword and the "AI" features were badly implemented. Two years on, the specs are frozen in amber, the AI associations are becoming negative for regular customers, and the "Copilot+ AI PC" era is dead. Windows Central's Zac Bowden reports the branding absent at a trade show last week.

At this year's Snapdragon Summit, I had the chance to ask Surface CVP Brett Ostrum about the lack of Copilot+ PC branding on its recent Surface PCs, and he confirmed that "these are not called Copilot+ PCs. They do meet all the requirements of our previous bar for what Copilot+ devices are. We still lean into the narrative around AI on the edge and being able to have a hybrid solution out there." I've also asked Qualcomm's SVP of compute, Kedar Kondap, about his thoughts on the usage of the Copilot+ PC branding. He told me that "the purpose for Copilot+ PCs was to be able to deliver [NPU] experiences. So it was to define a certain category of devices with a certain bar and metric, like for example, a 45 TOPS NPU … So from that perspective, it's more offering the same experiences, probably without just using [Copilot+ PC] terminology now."

Perhaps they wanted it thoroughly forgotten before Nvidia's upcoming RTX Spark devices start showing up. The leaked base spec is nothing to write home about, but the flagship models will be beasts.

Techspot's Daniel Sims called it when Dell revived its XPS branding and the RAM price crisis—itself driven by shortages caused by AI companies—forced Microsoft itself to put out new 8GB models that didn't meet the spec. "Nobody wants an AI PC," Sims writes.

One of the biggest signs came in January, when Dell revived the XPS brand after killing it a year earlier – admitting that AI alone isn't a good enough selling point for new PCs. Microsoft's latest Surface laptop refresh even includes models with only 8GB of RAM, meaning they no longer meet the original AI PC benchmark. Ironically, AI-driven memory shortages are partly to blame. Early next month, Microsoft plans to unveil new high-end Surface laptops in collaboration with Nvidia, which has historically preferred running AI workloads on its own RTX GPUs rather than NPUs.

text:
On September 10, 2026, Reuters reported that Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) plans to expand its global data center capacity to more than 38 gigawatts by 2032, more than tripling its current roughly 12-gigawatt footprint, according to Bloomberg News reporting that cited people familiar with the plans. Only about 2 gigawatts of Microsoft's current capacity is dedicated to AI-specific chips, a share the company expects to grow to roughly one-third of the much larger 38-gigawatt total by 2032, though Microsoft has not confirmed the target in any public filing or statement.

Don't Miss: Berkshire (BRK.B)'s CEO Says Communities Are Fighting Back on Data Centers

Bull Case

Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) already has strong cloud demand to support a major expansion of its data center footprint. Azure and other cloud services revenue increased 43% year over year in fiscal Q4. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $59.3 billion for the quarter and $214.4 billion for fiscal 2026. Microsoft also said capacity constraints have limited its ability to satisfy some demand, so expanding from roughly 12 gigawatts toward the reported 38-gigawatt target could allow the company to capture cloud and AI business that its existing infrastructure cannot currently support.

Microsoft's massive contracted backlog gives management substantial revenue visibility as it adds new computing capacity. Commercial remaining performance obligations increased 84% year over year to $678 billion, while Microsoft expects to recognize roughly 30% of that amount as revenue during the next 12 months. The large backlog gives Microsoft a significant pool of committed business that can help support the economics of its aggressive infrastructure expansion as new capacity comes online.

Microsoft has already shown that it can add capacity quickly while securing long-term power for its expanding data center network. The company added another gigawatt of capacity in fiscal Q4 and remains on track to roughly double its overall capacity within two years. Microsoft has also signed a 20-year agreement with Constellation Energy linked to the restart of the 835-megawatt Three Mile Island Unit 1. It gives the firm another long-term electricity source as AI workloads drive sharply higher power requirements.

Look Into: Alphabet (GOOGL)'s Google Bets on Finland's Cold Weather and Nuclear Power for its Next AI Buildout

Bear Case

Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)'s data center expansion requires enormous capital commitments that could continue weighing on free cash flow. Microsoft expects more than $50 billion of capital expenditures in fiscal Q1 2027 and about $175 billion during calendar 2026 under its broader capex definition, which includes finance leases. Microsoft reported roughly $145 billion of capital expenditures in fiscal 2026, while cash additions to property and equipment totaled about $116 billion.

Power availability and growing political resistance could make a 38-gigawatt network harder to build on schedule. Texas temporarily halted approvals for new data center grid connections as officials reviewed the industry's electricity and water demands. New York imposed a moratorium on large new data centers amid concerns about electricity costs. "I've heard concerns about companies using that information and technology to charge you more," Furner said. "I want to tell you where we stand: We price the product, not the person."

Furner said prices may fluctuate when the cost of goods or transportation changes, but stressed that Walmart will not use a customer's income, shopping history, urgency or other personal information to set prices.

WALMART LAUNCHES WEEKLONG FALL SALE OVERLAPPING AMAZON PRIME BIG DEAL DAYS

"We won’t do it," Furner said. "YOU are at the heart of our WHY and our relationship with you has always been built on trust. For decades, our associates have built that trust, one interaction at a time."

"So, as technology improves, we’re putting the same attention on trust and serving you as we do when you walk into our stores and clubs."

Furner also addressed Walmart's rollout of digital shelf labels, saying the technology is meant to improve price accuracy while reducing the amount of time that employees spend replacing paper tags.

"A shelf price should match what rings up at checkout. Digital shelf labels help us do that more consistently by displaying the right price," he said. "They also save associates time replacing paper tags."

WALMART AGREES TO PAY $50M SETTLEMENT OVER ALLEGATIONS ITS PHARMACIES FILLED ILLEGAL OPIOID PRESCRIPTIONS

Furner added, "It may sound like an easy task – but as someone who has had to change those paper tags by hand over the years, I can tell you it’s a time-consuming and unrewarding task."

title: OpenAI to Halt Training of Some Models - Gizmodo
authors: Tom McKay, John Loeffler, Mike Pearl, Webb Wright
description:
The Associated Press reported on Saturday evening that OpenAI acknowledged the pause in a statement, writing it would resume training the models “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” and expects to have to “hit pause” again.
Researchers with security firm Transluce have highlighted numerous incidents where OpenAI models aggressively probed websites for information, adding that in the Education instance, models made a rudimentary effort to break into the website of the department’s civil rights office.
Furious Australian politicians have demanded OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei show up in person for a legislative inquiry.
As the AP noted, President Donald Trump spent part of his time meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week coordinating on AI safety.
As the firm pursues ever more capable models, its compute infrastructure and training costs have skyrocketed.
text:
OpenAI has halted training of its latest AI models as reports of them “going rogue” stack up—including a cyberattack on AI platform Hugging Face, other attacks on third parties originating from security tests, and its agents probing government websites and, in at least one case, trying to break in.

The Associated Press reported on Saturday evening that OpenAI acknowledged the pause in a statement, writing it would resume training the models “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” and expects to have to “hit pause” again.

In the incidents involving U.S. government agencies—the Department of Education, the Commerce Department, and the Securities and Exchange Commission—spokespeople for the government have denied any significant impact. Researchers with security firm Transluce have highlighted numerous incidents where OpenAI models aggressively probed websites for information, adding that in the Education instance, models made a rudimentary effort to break into the website of the department’s civil rights office.

A separate string of incidents involving the Australian government and its Medicare program did involve a break-in and unauthorized access by OpenAI agents. Furious Australian politicians have demanded OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei show up in person for a legislative inquiry. According to Reuters, OpenAI also acknowledged on Friday its models uploaded 53 user images to the internet and that there had been internal disagreement about the effectiveness of its data anonymization processes.

Cybersecurity and legal experts generally agree—and AI leaders worry—that developers can and should be held accountable for their models’ action within reason. According to SecurityWeek, though, experts also say prosecutions may face an uphill battle in proving AI firms or their employees had acted so recklessly so as to be criminally liable.

The civil liability alone could be an existential threat to the industry, according to Palantir CEO Alex Karp, whose firm has partnerships with numerous AI developers. He argued in a CNBC appearance earlier this month that the current “AI safety” trend has less to do with safety than AI firms reckoning with the potential liabilities they might face as their tech rolls out across the entire economy.

As the AP noted, President Donald Trump spent part of his time meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week coordinating on AI safety. However, Trump afterwards denied that the U.S. would be “putting on the brakes,” adding that an unspecified “they” desire to “stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”

It’s worth noting that this push toward a training slowdown, in addition to perhaps giving OpenAI some breathing room to deal with the growing backlash, holds a silver lining for Altman and crew. As the firm pursues ever more capable models, its compute infrastructure and training costs have skyrocketed. TechRepublic reported the firm was, as of earlier this week, on track to burn through $280 billion by the end of 2030.

OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment from Gizmodo. We’ll update this post if and when we hear back, though.

title: OpenAI Pauses Training and Evaluation of Its 'Most Advanced Models' - PCMag
description:
OpenAI has now made the decision to pause training, evaluation and tool-using inference of its "most advanced models," amid a string of recent incidents where they broke containment.
OpenAI says its misalignment monitoring system flagged the behavior within 15 minutes and a human began reviewing it three minutes after that.
The incident above comes after OpenAI revealed earlier this week that its models accessed publicly available information on two websites operated by the Securities and Exchange Commission, as well as Census Bureau data accessed using publicly available developer keys.
OpenAI said it found no evidence of a compromise, credential misuse, or access to non-public information at the SEC or Census Bureau.
Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.
text:
AI alignment fears have never been more clearly in the spotlight, with OpenAI's Sam Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and SpaceX's Elon Musk all calling for an AI slowdown, and famous faces like former President Barack Obama even chiming in with agreement.

OpenAI has now made the decision to pause training, evaluation and tool-using inference of its "most advanced models," amid a string of recent incidents where they broke containment.

The AI giant made the recent move following an agent attempting to complete a search-based training task by querying a public chatbot service, exploiting a gap in its internet-access restrictions by abusing "insufficient Domain Name System (DNS) filtering" in its training sandbox.

The agent had previously issued queries via its search tool and unsuccessfully tried to access search engines directly, being unable to break through to the live internet. OpenAI says its misalignment monitoring system flagged the behavior within 15 minutes and a human began reviewing it three minutes after that. The run was killed 2.5 hours later. The agent had been tasked with identifying the author of a blog post, and was given a set of clues to start off its research.

"This incident is a lot less severe than some of our previous incidents, but because it's the first one since our security hardening following the Hugging Face incident, it gives us an important signal about where to focus the next phase of that work," OpenAI said in its incident report.

The incident above comes after OpenAI revealed earlier this week that its models accessed publicly available information on two websites operated by the Securities and Exchange Commission, as well as Census Bureau data accessed using publicly available developer keys.

OpenAI said it found no evidence of a compromise, credential misuse, or access to non-public information at the SEC or Census Bureau.

OpenAI also revealed earlier this week that its agents had posted 53 user-uploaded images to image-hosting sites, though the company maintains July's high-profile Hugging Face attack remains the most severe incident the company has seen.

Earlier this week, independent researchers at Transluce also reported that an agent unsuccessfully attempted to breach a Department of Education website tied to its Office for Civil Rights, though the department said it found no evidence of any impact to its website or databases.

Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.

Eli Lilly and Company (NYSE:LLY)'s CEO David Ricks told CNBC that Foundayo now accounts for roughly one-third of new patients starting an oral GLP-1, with Lilly's share of the pill market increasing week over week. The update comes as Lilly broke ground on a $6.5 billion manufacturing facility in Houston that is expected to be operational by 2030 and will produce Foundayo and other small-molecule medicines. Lilly also plans to launch Foundayo in additional international markets.

The early commercial traction is meaningful because Foundayo generated $98 million in second-quarter revenue after launching in April. Lilly's total revenue reached $23.0 billion in Q2, up 48% year over year, while the company raised its 2026 revenue guidance to $85 billion-$87 billion.

Also read: Foundayo's Early Growth Is Raising Lilly (LLY)'s Revenue Expectations. But Can It Outrun Pricing Pressure?

Foundayo's Growing Share Could Give Lilly Another Major Growth Driver

Foundayo could give Eli Lilly and Company (NYSE:LLY) another major growth engine in obesity while expanding the overall GLP-1 market. Lilly previously reported that about 80% of early Foundayo prescriptions were from patients new to the GLP-1 category, suggesting the pill is not simply shifting existing Zepbound users from injections. Reuters has also reported that oral GLP-1 drugs could capture as much as 40% of the market as pills attract patients who are reluctant to use injections.

The product also has characteristics that could support adoption. Foundayo can be taken once daily without food or water restrictions, while Lilly's clinical data showed up to 13% average weight reduction at the highest approved dose among adults aged 65 and older. Lilly has also reported that Foundayo outperformed oral semaglutide in a head-to-head diabetes trial on both A1C reduction and weight loss.

Lilly is building capacity ahead of potential demand rather than waiting for supply constraints to emerge. The company has already undertaken significant manufacturing expansion, including an additional $4.5 billion commitment to Indiana facilities, while the Houston project adds another $6.5 billion of long-term capacity. If Foundayo's market share continues rising and international launches broaden its reach, those investments could support larger volumes and extend Lilly's cardiometabolic growth beyond Zepbound and Mounjaro.

Foundayo Faces a Tougher Test as Oral GLP-1 Competition Accelerates

Foundayo's current contribution remains small relative to Eli Lilly and Company (NYSE:LLY)'s existing GLP-1 franchise. The pill generated only $98 million in Q2, while Mounjaro generated $9.94 billion and Zepbound generated $4.93 billion. Mounjaro and Zepbound together represented 65% of Lilly's revenue during the first half of 2026, meaning the company's near-term financial performance remains heavily dependent on its injectable products.

text:
Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) added a tool called Code to its Copilot app on September 25. It lets someone build an app or a dashboard by describing it in plain language. The technology underneath is not new. It is the same engine that powers GitHub Copilot, which developers have used for years. What has changed is who gets to point it at a problem.

Microsoft also embedded Word, Excel and PowerPoint directly inside Copilot, and relaunched its Scout agent as Autopilot. The shares rose 3.66% to close at $516.17.

READ ALSO: Microsoft (MSFT) Raises Its Dividend 8%. Does AI Spending Change the Investment Case?

Handing a Developer Tool to People Who Cannot Code:

GitHub Copilot was built for programmers. It sits inside a code editor; it assumes the user knows what a function is, and it speaks to an audience of developers.

Microsoft 365 is sold to whole organizations rather than to their engineering teams. Putting the same coding engine into the app everyone there already opens does not improve the tool. It multiplies the number of hands on it, reaching the finance department, the sales floor, and the operations desk.

That is the commercial idea. An accountant who wants a dashboard typically files a request with an IT department and waits. If Code works as advertised, that request never gets filed, and the accountant stays inside a Microsoft product while not filing it.

The agent change points the same way. Autopilot will carry its own identity in the company directory and hold permissions an administrator can set, which treats software as something closer to a colleague than a feature. Microsoft says governance and compliance worries have been the main obstacle to putting agents inside large organizations. Giving one a staff record and a controlled permission set answers that objection directly.

DON'T MISS: "The New Clippy": Benioff Uses Salesforce's Biggest Product Launch in Years to Challenge Microsoft

Almost None of This Has Shipped:

Here is the part the announcement does not lead with. Code reaches early access customers at the end of the month, and paying subscribers only get a preview later this year. Autopilot arrives as a private preview.

A preview is not revenue. Microsoft has announced Copilot improvements repeatedly over the past year, including a redesign earlier in 2026. Those announcements have not yet shown up in the revenue line, and the twelve-month share price has not rewarded them either, whatever Friday's reaction suggests.

That reflection is unflattering. Microsoft has gone essentially nowhere over the past twelve months and sits well below its 52-week high of $553.72, while several of the companies it competes with have run hard.

text:

It's been a busy week for Microsoft. Despite having a Windows and Surface event scheduled two weeks from now, the company announced two new Surface PCs and revived the Surface Mouse. Microsoft also effectively cut the legs out from under the Copilot+ PC brand by confirming the new Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch are not Copilot+ PCs.

Biggest News of the Week

Microsoft confirmed that its new Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch will not be called Copilot+ PCs. Not because they fail to meet the requirements — both PCs have the specs to otherwise qualify — but because Microsoft is going in a different direction.

I think we may hear more about Microsoft's plans and rebranding at the Windows and Surface event next month, but for now we just have confirmation the new Surface devices are not called Copilot+ PCs.

The Copilot+ PC brand was doomed to fail. Microsoft failed to make it clear to customers what made Copilot+ PCs special, and the flagship Recall was a disaster.

Many people were confused about the difference between a Copilot+ PC and an AI PC. And several major manufacturers made it clear that labeling a device as a Copilot+ PC was not a priority.

Too many Copilots

Microsoft put too many eggs in the same basket with Copilot. The company has dozens of products with Copilot in their names. Even the Microsoft 365 app had Copilot forced into its name.

By bundling so many different products and services under the Copilot name, Microsoft tied the success (or failure) of a large part of its portfolio together.

Look online for reactions to the Copilot+ PC brand being phased out and you'll see people discussing the Copilot app, the Copilot key, Microsoft 365 Copilot, and other Copilot-branded products. And who can blame them? It's natural to assume the end of Copilot+ PCs means the end of at least some parts of Copilot.

But the opposite is true. In the same week it confirmed its Surface PCs are not Copilot+ PCs, Microsoft announced a massive overhaul of the Copilot platform. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called it a new OS, though I'm not sure what that really means in this case.

Ultimately, Microsoft fell in love with the term Copilot and tried to attach it to too many products and services. We've seen similar mistakes, such as Facebook going all in on the Metaverse.

Copilot+ PCs are gone or being phased out, but Copilot as an "OS" is just beginning. Microsoft will need to do some damage control and get a marketing message out to make it clear those facts aren't in opposition.

title: Why Global MedTech Giants Are Now Betting on Costa Rica Over Asia for Smart Factories
description:
From Banana Republic to Smart Factory Hub The pivotal shift is not simply how much capital is reaching Costa Rica — it is what that capital is funding on the factory floor.
The Free Zone Machine — and Its Friction Costa Rica's free trade zone regime remains the engine powering much of this growth.
Houston, meanwhile, benefits from Costa Rica's growing electronics and semiconductor components sector, which connects into Gulf Coast industrial supply chains.
What Costa Rica is building is not a less expensive version of what Vietnam or Bangladesh offers.
Costa Rica is betting it can own that premium tier.
text:
From Banana Republic to Smart Factory Hub

The pivotal shift is not simply how much capital is reaching Costa Rica — it is what that capital is funding on the factory floor. Industry observers describe facilities that have moved well past basic assembly and now run predictive analytics platforms, AI-assisted inspection systems, and cloud-connected operations as part of routine daily production — a transformation that CINDE, Costa Rica's investment promotion agency, frames as the country's full entry into the Industry 4.0 era.

The transition is moving fastest in medtech. More than 90 multinational companies in the medical technology space call the country home — including 13 of the world's top 20 original equipment manufacturers — directly employing more than 62,000 workers and contributing 13% to GDP. Sector leaders Boston Scientific, Abbott Medical, Edwards Lifesciences, and Medtronic chose Costa Rica not because it offered the lowest unit cost, but because its engineers and technicians can manage compliance-intensive, highly regulated production environments that most Central American competitors cannot replicate.

That workforce advantage rests on a sustained national investment in STEM education that has built a deep pipeline of software engineers, automation specialists, and precision manufacturing technicians who increasingly work side by side with multinational R&D teams headquartered in the United States.

The Free Zone Machine — and Its Friction

Costa Rica's free trade zone regime remains the engine powering much of this growth. Free zones captured 64.9% of all inbound FDI during the first nine months of 2025, drawing investors with full import/export duty exemptions, streamlined customs clearance, and access to a broad network of trade agreements covering the U.S., European Union, and major Asian markets.

Evolution Free Zone — a 124-hectare high-tech business park in Tacares de Grecia, Alajuela, positioned outside the Greater Metropolitan Area with direct access to Route 1 and just 15 minutes from Juan Santamaría International Airport — has emerged as one of the country's most rapidly expanding new parks, explicitly targeting life sciences, smart manufacturing, and semiconductor companies seeking turnkey, high-specification facilities.

Yet 2026 has introduced significant headwinds. On July 24, the Trump administration formally imposed a 12.5% tariff on Costa Rican goods. The U.S. Trade Representative concluded that Costa Rica had neither established nor effectively enforced a legal prohibition on importing goods produced with forced labor — a determination the Costa Rican government vigorously disputed, arguing that the country's manufacturers reinforce rather than undercut U.S. production through integrated supply chains. The Section 301 action targeted more than 60 economies globally, with Costa Rica placed in the 12.5% bracket, though certain goods under CAFTA-DR provisions may qualify for exclusions.

What This Means for Miami, Houston, and the U.S. Logistics Corridor

The strategic angle for U.S. readers is not in San José — it is in the American distribution infrastructure that Costa Rica's manufacturing expansion feeds directly. The Inter-American Development Bank estimates nearshoring could generate up to $78 billion in additional annual exports of goods and services across Latin America and the Caribbean, and a significant share of that cargo already moves through Miami International Airport and the Port of Miami — both deeply integrated into Costa Rica's medtech and precision electronics export chains.

For South Florida's logistics sector, every new multinational production hub established in the Central Valley generates downstream demand for freight forwarding, customs brokerage, cold-chain warehousing, and last-mile distribution that feeds directly into Miami-Dade employment. Houston, meanwhile, benefits from Costa Rica's growing electronics and semiconductor components sector, which connects into Gulf Coast industrial supply chains.

This bilateral flow is also reshaping what types of roles Latin American workers in the United States are being trained and recruited to fill — not warehouse packers, but supply chain analysts, quality compliance coordinators, and bilingual operations managers who understand both the production environment in Alajuela and the regulatory demands of U.S.-based buyers.

The Bigger Strategic Bet

Costa Rica is making a deliberate wager that the next phase of nearshoring competition will not be decided by unit labor cost. The country generated 98.6% of its electricity from renewable sources in 2025 — a grid powered by hydroelectric, geothermal, wind, biomass, and solar installations — and holds internationally recognized carbon neutrality certifications that are becoming concrete procurement factors as U.S. multinationals face ESG reporting requirements from their own investors.

What Costa Rica is building is not a less expensive version of what Vietnam or Bangladesh offers. It is a different proposition entirely: stable, sustainable, technically sophisticated manufacturing infrastructure that sits in the same time zone as New York, lies under three hours by air from Miami, and operates inside a democratic legal framework undisturbed by a military coup for more than 75 years.

Regional analysts note that competition is intensifying — the Dominican Republic and Mexico are both expanding their medical device manufacturing footprints — and infrastructure bottlenecks remain a genuine constraint on how fast Costa Rica can scale. But the underlying logic holds: when geopolitical disruption makes "cheapest" an unreliable planning variable, "most reliable" becomes the premium multinationals will pay for.

Costa Rica is betting it can own that premium tier. The capital flowing in suggests it already does.

text:
By Britney Nguyen and Bill Peters

Micron is increasingly important to the S&P 500, and its earnings report has become 'a market event in and of itself'

Micron Technology reports earnings on Wednesday.

Micron Technology may be about to steal Nvidia's thunder and underscore its increasing relevance to the broader stock market.

When the memory-chip maker reports earnings on Wednesday, it's expected to deliver major profit growth. Analysts tracked by FactSet expect earnings per share to have rocketed 940% higher in the August quarter relative to a year before.

The results for Micron (MU) will arrive as the artificial-intelligence boom gobbles up memory-chip supplies and squeezes prices higher, creating a profit windfall for the company. And if analysts' predictions hold, it would mark the first time in at least two-and-a-half years that Micron manages to dethrone Nvidia (NVDA) and its Big Tech peers to become the leading contributor to the S&P 500's SPX profit growth, according to data from Seaport Research Partners.

Micron's stock has made a 279% run higher so far this year, although shares have had their ups and downs over the past three months. The company has a $1.2 trillion market valuation, and its results are closely watched as a gauge of AI demand.

The company sits at the intersection of two of the market's main themes: the durability of AI spending and a recent concentration in market leadership, Jake Behan, Direxion's head of capital markets, told MarketWatch. Against that backdrop, the stock is one of a handful of companies that's driven the Nasdaq Composite COMP to all-time highs.

"When you have leadership that's this narrow, it stops being company-specific, and the report becomes a market event in and of itself," Behan said. Micron's stock has "become a referendum on the health of the AI build-out," he added.

Moreover, Jacob Bourne, a technology analyst at Emarketer, told MarketWatch that Micron's results "should offer a useful indication of whether strength is broadening beyond AI infrastructure."

The stock market this year has battled concerns surrounding the cost of the AI build-out. Goldman Sachs analysts last month said they expect global AI investment to surpass $1 trillion this year, as big U.S. cloud providers including Amazon.com (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG) and Microsoft (MSFT) shovel billions of dollars into data centers and other technology.

Micron's influence on the S&P 500 has been building over the past year. During last year's third quarter, Micron was the ninth-biggest contributor to the index's earnings growth, according to FactSet. As the memory crunch deepened, its rank rose to sixth in last year's fourth quarter, then third over the first half of this year.

While Micron's earnings report doesn't align with the usual calendar schedule that other companies follow, FactSet considers the company's results to be part of the third quarter. The chip maker's report will land before the third-quarter earnings season really kicks into gear next month.

For now, analysts expect S&P 500 earnings to grow 29.1% for the third quarter, according to FactSet. Factor out Micron, and that growth drops to 24%, according to the research firm. But that would still mark the eighth straight quarter of double-digit earnings gains for the benchmark index.

"Even if you threw Micron out of the S&P, the earnings growth is still insanely good," said Jonathan Golub, chief investment strategist at Seaport Research Partners.

-Britney Nguyen -Bill Peters

title: When Do You Start Paying Attention? A Lesson from NVIDIA's 2018 Financial Results
description:
Without that 2017 paper, there is no ChatGPT, no Claude, no Astra and no coherent story for why NVIDIA’s data center revenue went where it went.
The lesson is not “brilliant papers always compound into trillion-dollar outcomes.” The lesson is narrower and potentially more useful.

It does not tell us when, or even whether, quantum computing crosses from research curiosity to commercial inflection.
NVIDIA’s stock did not wait for fiscal 2026 revenue to be reported before it moved.
text:
The Number That Started This

In fiscal 2018, which was the year ended January 28, 2018, NVIDIA generated $9.71 billion in revenue.1 By fiscal 2026, ended January 25, 2026, that figure had reached $215.94 billion.2 That is roughly 22 times larger, a compound annual growth rate of approximately 47% sustained over eight consecutive years.

To put a finer point on it, NVIDIA’s fourth-quarter revenue alone in fiscal 2026, $68.1 billion, was about seven times the company’s entire annual revenue eight years earlier.3

I did not pick 2018 as a starting point at random. That was the year when WisdomTree, globally speaking, began treating artificial intelligence as a distinct, investable theme. We were not early by the standards of Silicon Valley insiders, but we were early relative to the broad market’s eventual embrace of the idea. What strikes me now, looking back, is how little of the technical foundation for what actually happened was visible to us, or to almost anyone outside a narrow research community, at that moment.

The Paper Nobody Outside the Field Was Reading

In June 2017, eight researchers at Google published a paper titled “Attention Is All You Need.”4 It introduced the Transformer architecture, which is a way of processing sequences using only attention mechanisms, discarding the recurrent and convolutional structures that had dominated natural language processing until then. The paper is, by later standards, almost modest—just eight pages, a translation benchmark and a somewhat cheeky title.

It is also the architecture underneath essentially every large language model that exists today. GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer. The “T” is not incidental. Without that 2017 paper, there is no ChatGPT, no Claude, no Astra and no coherent story for why NVIDIA’s data center revenue went where it went.

ChatGPT launched to the public on November 30, 2022.5 That is roughly five and a half years after the Transformer paper appeared. For almost all of that interval, the idea existed, the architecture existed, researchers were building on it, and the broader investing public had no reason to notice. There was no product, no headline and no obvious reason for revenue to move. The scale-up that mattered, meaning the compute, the data and the engineering to turn an architecture into a consumer-facing capability, happened quietly, in a window most of us were not watching.

I want to be careful here, because I think this is exactly the point where reasoning like mine tends to go wrong.

It is tempting, in hindsight, to make the story sound more inevitable than it was.

Plenty of architectures and papers from that era went nowhere. The Transformer was not obviously “the one” in 2017, even to many people working adjacent to it. The lesson is not “brilliant papers always compound into trillion-dollar outcomes.” The lesson is narrower and potentially more useful.

Transformative technological shifts are frequently preceded by a multi-year period in which the foundational science is published, understood by specialists and essentially invisible to everyone else, including to capital markets.

Sign me up to receive email newsletters from VettaFi Advisor Perspectives

Where This Leaves Quantum Computing

I do not know whether quantum computing is in that kind of window right now. Nobody does, and I am suspicious of anyone who claims certainty in either direction. What I can say is that the pattern-matching is uncomfortably familiar. Over the past two years, the research coming out of groups working on error correction, logical qubits and specific problem classes, be it cryptography, chemistry or optimization to name a few, has moved from “interesting in principle” to “here is a specific, falsifiable claim about what a machine with N logical qubits could do.” Much of it is still confined to papers, preprints and specialist conferences. Very little of it has produced a headline that reaches a general audience the way ChatGPT did in November 2022.

That gap, between what is happening in the research literature and what is visible to the broader market, is precisely the gap that existed for transformers between 2017 and roughly 2022. It does not tell us when, or even whether, quantum computing crosses from research curiosity to commercial inflection. Revenue for the sector today is a rounding error next to NVIDIA’s, and the hardware challenges are arguably harder than anything language models faced. But the structural shape of “quiet research phase, then a scale-up that becomes visible all at once” is a pattern worth taking seriously precisely because we have just watched it happen, in real time, with a company whose income statement we can all pull up.

What This Actually Argues For

I am not arguing for a specific quantum computing trade, and I do not think this framework tells you which company, if any, becomes the “NVIDIA of quantum computing.” What it argues for is something more basic.

In my view, it argues for paying attention during the quiet phase, before the evidence is obvious, because the evidence tends to become obvious only after most of the value has already been created.

NVIDIA’s stock did not wait for fiscal 2026 revenue to be reported before it moved. By the time $215.94 billion showed up on an income statement, the repricing had largely already happened.

If there is a lesson in the 2018-to-2026 numbers, it is not “predict the future.” It is “notice which parts of your own research process would have caught this the first time, and are you running that process now, on the fields where you genuinely do not yet know the answer.” Quantum computing could be one candidate.

1 Source: NVIDIA Corporation. (2018). Annual report (Form 10-K) for the fiscal year ended January 28, 2018. U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

2 Source: NVIDIA Corporation. (2026). Annual report (Form 10-K) for the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026. U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

3 Source: NVIDIA Corporation, 2026.

4 Source: Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention is all you need. arXiv.

5 Source: OpenAI. (2022, November 30). Introducing ChatGPT.

Airbnb has gone through several false starts with its experiences business, first launched more than a decade ago. It has relaxed its long-held resistance to high-demand mainstream tours of landmarks like the Eiffel Tower. But now the question is whether it can succeed by marketing to locals — something few other experiences companies have found success with.

Airbnb relaunched experiences in 2025 and after a sluggish start, CEO Brian Chesky has said the company wanted to focus on getting one city right — Paris. The focus is paying off, Chesky said last week at the Skift Global Forum, with growth "6x year over year."

"One of the reasons they're growing is we've now started to crack locals," Chesky said. "Locals in Paris are booking experiences in Paris, something we never thought would happen, so now we're taking that playbook to New York and other cities. And I think we're not even close to that happening in 1,000 cities but I think that will happen soon."

text:
OpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount.

The decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.

Separately, the AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a US Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.

OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge.

Last week Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, revealed an OpenAI agent had breached the government’s national healthcare system – but said no sensitive information had been compromised.

AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own, hacking websites and disclosing nonpublic information. The heads of both OpenAI and rival Anthropic have called for a slowdown too.

It is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first came in July after disclosure of a cyber-attack targeting AI startup Hugging Face, a now notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.

In a meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping this week, Donald Trump agreed to share information on AI dangers and coordinate efforts to keep it safe. Trump believes AI fears are overblown, though, and later suggested that he plans no crackdown of his own.

The US is not going to be “putting on brakes”, Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They want to stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”

The latest OpenAI incidents did not appear to involve the disclosure of any nonpublic information but were concerning enough for the company to warn the federal agencies involved.

In the education department incident, OpenAI agents found API “developer keys” to access government data, though ultimately only publicly available information was gathered.

In another case involving the securities and exchange commission, agents found information freely available to all but then posted it elsewhere on the internet, an act that went beyond what they were instructed to do.

US Securities and Exchange Commission spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said on Saturday that “no nonpublic information was accessed”.

The Department of Education said earlier that it found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases”.

Several other AI companies have disclosed incidents of their models going rogue and even hacking websites.

OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, said in a social media post on Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen”.

OpenAI previously shared six other reports of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances.

Some may recall that in January 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang predicted a long wait, up to 30 years, for "very useful" quantum computers. That comment roiled quantum stocks across the board, with IonQ, Inc. (NYSE:IONQ) shares plunging about 40% in their worst single-day drop.

To be fair, commercially useful, fault-tolerant, quantum computers, have not arrived yet. But less than two years later, IonQ has secured a prominent role in Nvidia's push to develop useful hybrid quantum-classical systems. IonQ said on September 23 that its Superion 256 will become the first on-premise quantum processor deployed at Nvidia's Accelerated Quantum Research Center (NVAQC). The deployment is planned for 2027.

That's a big deal.

Also Read: IonQ (IONQ) Just Posted Record Results, So Why Is The Stock Still Down?

IonQ's Roadmap Just Got Stronger

The Nvidia partnership provides a tangible testing ground for IonQ's Superion architecture. Nvidia will place IonQ, Inc. (NYSE:IONQ)'s quantum processing unit alongside conventional accelerated computing hardware. That will happen in a setting specifically designed to develop large-scale hybrid systems. The research will target applications including financial optimization, materials science and computational chemistry.

IonQ introduced Superion 256 on September 8, and the company has begun accepting orders. First customer deliveries are expected in 2027, and the company is targeting commercially manufacturable fault-tolerant systems in 2028.

Beyond securing a prominent Nvidia research deployment, IonQ has also made important progress in advancing its quantum technology. On September 22, the company reported a decoder breakthrough aimed at removing a major bottleneck in quantum error correction.

IonQ demonstrated a real-time decoder capable of running continuously on a single conventional CPU. Its testing covered benchmark circuits simulating up to 408 logical qubits and more than 31.5 million quantum operations, with as little as 0.02% additional execution time.

IonQ did not demonstrate a physical quantum computer operating with 408 logical qubits. Instead, it tested whether a conventional processor could keep pace with the error-correction workload at that simulated scale. The result is relevant to the hybrid architecture that IonQ will test with Nvidia, where conventional processors support the quantum system.

IonQ Still Has a Lot to Prove

While the company's technology milestones shed more light into its opportunities, they don't immediately establish commercial economics. For instance, the financial value of the Nvidia deployment has not been disclosed. Additionally, Nvidia is working with multiple quantum companies.

IonQ, Inc. (NYSE:IONQ)'s 2026 revenue guidance of $450 million to $460 million also requires careful interpretation. The updated forecast includes SkyWater revenue from July 31 through year-end. So the increase cannot be attributed entirely to accelerating organic quantum-computing revenue.

Hedge Funds Expand Their Base as Shorts Shrink Theirs

IonQ, Inc. (NYSE:IONQ)'s hedge fund holders increased to 42 in Q2 from 39 in Q1 and 28 in Q4. D.E. Shaw, the top holder, raised its stake by 42%. Short interest declined to 10.83% of the float, from 11.2% in the previous reading.

The Nvidia deployment, together with the error-correction work, provides measurable milestones along the commercial roadmap. Investors will be watching to see how quickly IonQ moves Superion from technological demonstrations into paying-customer deployments.

text:
Bettina Orlopp has given the clearest account yet of how Commerzbank's standoff with UniCredit could end, telling Reuters that every option remains live. The Frankfurt lender's chief executive sketched a menu that runs from an outright acquisition to near-total integration, signaling that talks with the Milan-based group are still fluid more than a month after UniCredit's offer for its German rival.

At the top of Orlopp's list is a share-swap purchase of HypoVereinsbank, UniCredit's German subsidiary. Such a deal would deepen Commerzbank's domestic footprint while leaving it independent. A straight merger of the two banking groups forms the second path. The third would see UniCredit pitch a premium offer to Commerzbank's remaining shareholders, lifting its stake above 90% and clearing the way for a squeeze-out.

UniCredit has already locked up access to as much as 49.65% of Commerzbank's voting rights, though that transition still hinges on regulatory approvals. Berlin, meanwhile, continues to watch the maneuvering with a wary eye. Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil set out the government's expectations in mid-September during a meeting with UniCredit chief Andrea Orcel, pressing for the preservation of Commerzbank's German identity, its stock-market listing, and safeguards for jobs and lending to the country's small and mid-sized businesses.

Commerzbank's own positioning, published on 18 September, struck a conciliatory note, saying it sought talks on equal terms and viewed constructive dialogue as the right route to a durably value-creating outcome. Orlopp reinforced that message on Friday, arguing the bank must generate still more value for its shareholders and confirming it intends to keep its Swiss operations. Media reports suggest preparatory work is under way for a possible extraordinary shareholder meeting, which could serve as the forum for deciding how to handle the Italian anchor investor.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Commerzbank?

Buyback Rolls On as Analysts Turn More Constructive

Strategic questions have not slowed the bank's capital-return machine. At the start of September the board approved a buyback worth up to EUR 1.2 billion, launched the following day and scheduled to finish no later than 10 February 2027. Subject to approval by the European Central Bank and the German finance agency, the repurchased shares are to be cancelled. The program sits within an overall capital return of roughly EUR 3.2 billion targeted for the 2026 financial year.

Analysts see operational support beneath the stock. JPMorgan raised its price target on 8 September to EUR 39.00 from EUR 38.00, keeping a "Neutral" rating, and pointed to euro-area interest-rate trends as a tailwind for net interest income.

The market has been receptive to Frankfurt's conciliatory tone. Commerzbank shares closed Friday at EUR 42.39, a gain of 1.9%, leaving the stock just 2.2% below its 52-week high of EUR 43.34. Since the UniCredit offer more than a month ago, the equity has advanced 14.1%. Shareholder registers also shifted on Friday, with Commerzbank publishing a voting-rights notification from Japan's Nomura Holdings and a separate disclosure from US financial firm Jefferies Financial Group. Investors will get their next hard look at the underlying business on 5 November, the scheduled date for third-quarter 2026 results.

For shareholders, the decisive question is whether UniCredit opts for a formal premium offer or the discussions drift toward a partnership-style structure.

text:
NEW YORK (AP) — OpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount.

The decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.

Separately, AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.

OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge.

AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own, hacking websites and disclosing nonpublic information. The heads of both OpenAI and rival Anthropic have called for a slowdown too.

It is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first came in July after disclosure of a cyberattack targeting AI startup Hugging Face, a now notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.

In a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, President Donald Trump agreed to share information on AI dangers and coordinate efforts to keep it safe. Trump believes AI fears are overblown, though, and later suggested that he plans no crackdown of his own.

The U.S. is not going to be “putting on brakes,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They want to stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”

The latest OpenAI incidents did not appear to involve the disclosure of any nonpublic information but were concerning enough for the company to warn the federal agencies involved.

In the Department of Education incident, OpenAI agents found API “developer keys” to access government data, though ultimately only publicly available information was gathered.

In another case involving the Securities and Exchange Commission, agents found information freely available to all but then posted it elsewhere on the internet, an act that went beyond what they were instructed to do.

SEC spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said Saturday that “no nonpublic information was accessed.”

The Department of Education said earlier that it found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases.”

Several other AI companies have disclosed incidents of their models going rogue and even hacking websites.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a social media post Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen.”

Big pharma’s dealmaking appetite remains strong in 2026, but the strategic logic has shifted decisively toward platform access over outright company acquisitions.

Eli Lilly & Co (NYSE: LLY) and China’s InnoCare Pharma signed a research collaboration and license agreement on Thursday covering up to five undisclosed targets across cancer and autoimmune disease.

InnoCare is eligible to receive as much as $100 million in upfront and near-term payments, with an additional $3.25 billion available through development and commercial milestones, plus single-digit royalties.

The deal adds another China-origin discovery alliance to Lilly’s roster, continuing a year that has already been crowded with acquisitions and licensing activity for the Indianapolis-based drugmaker.

Novo Nordisk (NYSE: NVO) struck a separate platform deal, licensing Nanexa’s PharmaShell coating technology for long-acting peptide injectables targeting obesity, type 2 diabetes and other cardiometabolic conditions.

The exclusive global agreement covers up to five programs aimed at achieving monthly or quarterly dosing intervals, with Novo taking full responsibility for development and commercial operations.

Nanexa stands to earn up to €1.165 billion, equivalent to roughly $1.33 billion, including €615 million in upfront payments and development and regulatory milestones, along with low single-digit royalties.

AbbVie (NYSE: ABBV) launched a multi-year AI-driven drug discovery alliance with Iambic, targeting small molecules across immunology, neuroscience and oncology, with Iambic receiving an undisclosed upfront payment plus milestones and royalties.

Iambic filed for a Nasdaq IPO during the same week it announced the AbbVie collaboration, signaling growing investor confidence in AI-native drug discovery businesses.

Novartis (NYSE: NVS) rounded out the week’s activity by licensing a preclinical radioligand therapy from BoomRay in a deal valued at up to $900 million plus royalties, with the upfront payment left undisclosed.

This week’s transactions were notably smaller and more modular than the blockbuster company-buying wave that defined the opening months of 2026, when AstraZeneca licensed eight obesity and diabetes programs from China’s CSPC for up to $18.5 billion.

February and March then saw full-scale takeovers dominate the headlines, with Gilead paying approximately $7.8 billion for Arcellx’s late-stage CAR-T franchise, Lilly committing up to $7.8 billion for Centessa’s orexin sleep drugs, and Merck bidding $6.7 billion for Terns.

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around LLY was neutral at the time of publication, while sentiment around NVO was described as extremely bullish despite the stock falling 24% year-to-date.

Sentiment around both ABBV and NVS trended bearish, even as ABBV has gained 16% year-to-date and NVS has added 6% over the same period.

The SPDR S&P Biotech ETF (NYSE: XBI) has surged 27% in 2026, though it pulled back 2.5% during the week that these platform deals were announced.

A few hours after we wrote about Microsoft merging the Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot identities, CEO Satya Nadella revealed what Redmond wants this unified Copilot to become. The company unveiled its biggest Copilot update yet, bringing Home, Code, and Autopilot into one app while also adding Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside the “super app”.

In his typical pragmatic style, Nadella mentioned Copilot as a “new OS for work” spanning models, devices, and tasks, and we can’t help but remember how the company pitched Windows as becoming an “agentic OS” just a year ago, which triggered a major backlash from Windows users, forcing Windows chief Pavan Davuluri to lock replies on his post.

Either Redmond has stopped caring about the backlash, like how they recently unbanned “Microslop”, or they believe Copilot is finally good enough to earn a reputation for itself.

Well, from the looks of it, it’s the latter that fits the picture, and as of writing, Nadella’s post had already crossed one million views.

Satya Nadella says Copilot is a “new OS for work”

Without mentioning Windows 11 even once, Nadella says: “We’re building Copilot as a new OS for work that spans every model, every form factor, and every task.”

Yes, the new Copilot update is massive, and it’s not a chatbot anymore. But why mention it as an OS? Well, Microsoft believes that, just like an OS, the Copilot app, with its four new big additions, can essentially be the one-stop destination to get your work done.

Home is where you can get started, with Chat and Cowork.

Office apps, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, can now be used inside Copilot.

Code helps you build apps using Copilot and host them in your company tenant.

Autopilot is the full-blown agent that takes your goals and just keeps working.

Home will have your recent activity, suggestions, and a way to resume work already started. Chat is where you can ask quick questions and draft; Cowork handles delegated, multi-step work, and Microsoft says Copilot will eventually route a request between Chat, Cowork, and Code automatically instead of making you pick the mode yourself, which is huge if true!

Word, Excel, and PowerPoint are full apps inside Copilot. Whatever changes you make to any document or spreadsheet will be synced with the normal Office apps, and colleagues can keep editing the files as usual.

Home also gets Today, which shows relevant emails, meetings, Teams conversations, and tasks without you asking. This is what I always had in mind when thinking about an AI assistant.

Code turns Copilot into an app builder

Microsoft is not positioning the new Copilot Code feature for programmers only. The idea is that you can describe an app, tracker, dashboard, or workflow in plain English, and Copilot builds it.

Until now, to share an idea, we used to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations. They are a part of our muscle memory. Now, with Code, Microsoft expects us to add a fourth object by giving us the ability to create small applications built for specific jobs, like desktop widgets for quick reference or interactive dashboards.

Code runs on the same technology powering GitHub Copilot, executes inside a sandbox, and can be hosted inside a company’s own tenant through Copilot Managed Runtime. Microsoft IQ supplies business context, and plugins connect the app to relevant company data.

When Microsoft’s Distinguished Engineer David Fowler said “typing code is absolutely over”, this was where it was headed. Microsoft is making it as easy as possible for anyone, and we recently spotted them letting Copilot scaffold native WinUI apps in about 30 minutes.

Of course, we have to take everything with a grain of salt, because even as Microsoft says Code “lets everyone build their own solutions,” access is still rolling out, and we don’t have testing data yet.

Autopilot is like a colleague

Autopilot was previously called Scout, which Microsoft introduced at Build. You can give an Autopilot a name, a role, and a goal, and it can monitor channels, follow up on conversations, run recurring work, and pick a project back up days later.

Note that Autopilot runs in the cloud inside a company’s Microsoft 365 environment, with its own identity, memory, computer, and workspace. It can appear in Teams, Outlook, channels, and documents, and gets tagged like a colleague, with permissions, auditing, and governance, all under the organization’s control through Agent 365.

Autopilot grew out of Microsoft’s work on OpenClaw, the open-source personal AI agent that went viral earlier this year. Funnily enough, Nadella once compared it to “a virus”

With Autopilot, though, Microsoft is taking the useful idea behind persistent personal agents and allowing enterprises to properly govern it.

Microsoft was racing the clock to ship the new Copilot app before September ended

At Build 2026 in June, Nadella said Microsoft would bring Chat, Cowork, and Code together in one Copilot super app by summer.

On the July 29 earnings call, he told investors the pieces would come together this quarter, which ends September 30. Sure, the September 25, Friday announcement met the deadline, but most of what got announced is still arriving in pieces.

Code expands within Frontier at the end of the month, Autopilot enters private preview at the end of September, and Office in Copilot rolls out to consumers and Frontier customers in the coming weeks.

Copilot now has a new pricing model because autonomous AI costs more

If you want to know how much the new Copilot experience costs, start with finding how much of it you’ll need, because Copilot now bills two different ways.

A normal per-user subscription covers everyday use, including Chat and Copilot inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams, with model selection handled automatically.

The more expensive agentic workloads, Cowork, Code, and Autopilot, along with frontier models like OpenAI’s Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Fable, run on usage-based billing.

Usage-based services are off by default, and admins can set spending limits through Microsoft’s FinOps tools. The company is moving to a pay for the work the agent performs model, which is what Nadella previewed on the July earnings call.

Microsoft is finally catching up with the AI apps that stopped being chatbots

In less than 2 years, the AI industry has already moved fast in this direction. OpenAI’s Codex now supports long-running coding work and multi-agent workflows through its Agents API. Anthropic added Cowork and Claude Code, with Claude able to work across Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and other business files.

Even Google pushed Gemini toward computer use and background agents, with more to come as they bet on the new Googlebook laptops, which also featured Microsoft Copilot.

Interestingly, Microsoft was early to the AI assistant race but took the biggest brunt of the blame, leading to worldwide backlash. A user commented the same concerns I have: “You’ll be first to adopt every new technology but scaling it always proves a problem.”

Microsoft’s new OS for work isn’t Windows 12

I didn’t find any mock-up with the Windows 11 UI in the whole Copilot announcement. What changed here is that Microsoft replaced the existing chatbot-style Copilot application with Home, Code, Autopilot, and Office integration.

There is no OS here, but if you fancy seeing one, the leaked Project Aion was a Copilot-centric OS concept Microsoft explored in 2024, running on a stripped-down codebase called Win3 with no Start menu, no desktop icons, and a shell built inside a modified version of Edge.

Microsoft is trying to change what people think an AI application is. And surprisingly, Satya Nadella’s post didn’t see a backlash like the company’s posts used to get about a year ago.

What do you think about “Copilot” now?
